What’s triggering that dashboard warning light? 🚗⚠️ Explore 6 common car warning lights and possible causes in this quick animated guide.

From the check engine light to the power steering warning, this visual breakdown highlights components and conditions that may be involved:

🔴 CHECK ENGINE LIGHT
Spark plug problems, faulty ignition coils, or mass airflow (MAF) sensor issues are among the possible causes.

🔵 BATTERY / CHARGING SYSTEM WARNING
Charging problems may involve the alternator, serpentine belt, battery connections, or related electrical faults. This light does not automatically mean the battery needs replacement.

🟢 OIL PRESSURE WARNING
Possible causes include low oil level, oil pump problems, or an oil pressure sensor fault. Low oil pressure and low oil level are not the same thing.

🟠 ABS WARNING LIGHT
Potential causes include a wheel speed sensor, damaged reluctor ring, wiring fault, or ABS module problem.

🟣 ENGINE TEMPERATURE WARNING
Overheating may involve the thermostat, water pump, cooling fan, low coolant, or a leak.

🔷 POWER STEERING WARNING
Depending on the vehicle, possible causes include sensor faults, an electric power steering (EPS) motor or module problem, or an electrical supply issue.

⚠️ These are examples—not a complete diagnosis or a parts replacement checklist. A warning light alone cannot identify the failed component. Follow your owner’s manual and have the vehicle properly diagnosed.

If the oil pressure or engine temperature warning appears while driving, pull over safely and shut off the engine. Never open a hot cooling-system cap.

items.video_title: Dashboard Warning Lights Meaning
items.video_description:
The electronics system in today's cars relies on sensors attached to warning lights and symbols on the dashboard. There are two main types of dashboard warning lights available red and orange. A red warning light usually indicates a severe problem with your car. If your dashboard warning light is red, you should act quickly. 

An orange or yellow dashboard warning light means the Engine Management system - the computer running the engine - has detected a malfunction. You can continue to drive a car with an orange dashboard warning light, but you should visit your local service center as soon as possible for diagnosis and repair.

A Green or Blue dashboard light lets you know the system is on and operating.

FOG LIGHTS
The fog light symbol looks a lot like the one used for the regular headlights, albeit with a squiggly line in front of it instead of three lines that look like beams. Not all cars come equipped with fog lights, though, so it's possible you'll never see this dashboard light during the course of vehicle ownership.

LOW TIRE PRESSURE 
Modern cars come with  tire pressure monitoring systems and the little exclamation point inside of a half-circle merely means one or more of your tires have low pressure. If you see this sign don't freak out. Instead, find a safe place to stop and inspect your tires. If they look a bit low, carefully make your way to the nearest gas station to fill them with air. On most cars, this light will go away on its own after you've topped the tires off.

ENGINE OIL WARNING LIGHT 
Cars have been able to monitor their engine's oil pressure for years now. If you've seen what looks like a gravy boat light pop up in your dash it means there's a problem with your engine oil pressure. Without sufficient oil pressure, the engine can't properly lubricate itself. That can lead to major mechanical problems—the engine could seize and leave you stranded. As a result, it's best if you get this checked out right away.

CHECK ENGINE LIGHT 
The check engine light means that one of the many sensors monitoring your car has noticed a problem with the engine. It can be anything from a spark plug fault to the failure of something major such as the intake manifold or low compression. Unless you're really handy, you should leave a fix like this to a mechanic you trust. Either way, if you see the check engine light on your dash, something's gone wrong and you shouldn't put off a trip to the shop. The sooner you can fix it, the better.

COOLANT LEVEL WARNING LIGHT 
If you see a little thermometer pop up in your dash, that means your car is probably overheating. There are a number of things that could have happened, but the best thing to do is stop the car and wait a good long while for the engine to cool down by itself. Next, grab a rag, pop the hood, and use the rag to lift the lid of the coolant reservoir and check the coolant level. If your car is so hot the engine, coolant reservoir, or coolant tank is "smoking," then you might want to call a tow service.

BRAKE SYSTEM WARNING LIGHT 
In the event that you see an exclamation mark with a circle around it in your dash, that means something is wrong with your brakes. There may be a problem with brake components or the hydraulic fluid may need a top-off. Stop the car and call a tow truck as soon as you safely can. Driving without a fully functioning brake system is dangerous (not to mention totally nuts) and should be fixed as soon as possible.

ABS SENSOR WARNING LIGHT 
Although it is related to the braking system, the ABS warning light does not signal a failure of the physical brakes. Instead, this signals an issue with the anti-lock brake system. It's likely that if you stop too hard with this light on, then your car's brakes may lock up, which could make it a struggle to come to a full stop. It's best to take your car to a shop in this case, as ABS is one of the most important safety enhancements in cars since the  seatbelt was invented .

AIRBAG WARNING LIGHT 
All cars have airbags these days. It's federally mandated (as it should be), and sometimes you'll see an airbag warning light in your dash. This light can mean a number of things. It can indicate a problem with any number of items, including the sensors that detect crashes and deploy airbags in the event of an accident have failed. If this light pops up on your dash consistently, then it's time to take your car to a shop for a lookover.

BATTERY LIGHT 
If you see a little red battery on your dash, then that means you're currently powering your car on the battery alone. When the engine isn't on, the alternator isn't actively charging the battery. That means eventually you'll drain the battery and you'll likely need a jumpstart to get you going again. If this light is on while your car's engine is on, then it's typically a sign that the battery charging system isn't working. In that case, you're going to have to take your car somewhere to get the problem diagnosed.

items.video_description:
🚘 Have you ever wondered what those warning lights on your car's dashboard actually mean?

Understanding these symbols can help you identify potential vehicle problems and take timely action.

⚙️ 8 Common Dashboard Warning Lights:

1. Check Engine Light: Indicates a possible engine or emissions system issue.
2. EPC Light: Electronic Power Control warning, commonly found in certain vehicles.
3. ABS Light: Indicates a possible problem with the Anti-lock Braking System.
4. Traction Control Light: Indicates traction control activity or a system fault, depending on the symbol.
5. TPMS Light: Warns about low tyre pressure or a tyre pressure monitoring system fault.
6. Engine Temperature Light: Warns about excessive engine temperature.
7. Airbag Light: Indicates a possible fault in the airbag or supplemental restraint system.
8. Power Steering Light: Indicates a possible problem with the electric or hydraulic power steering system.

💡 Important:

- Red warning lights generally require immediate attention.
- Amber or yellow lights usually indicate a warning that needs checking.
- Never ignore an overheating warning or brake-related warning.

Test Battery Voltage, Make Sure Is Normal [Plate Redacted].4 V Or No More Than 12.6V. Also, Test For Battery Amperage. Amperage Is Written On Battery Label. If, After Testing Battery Amps Is Less Than The One Rated On The Battery, The Battery Must Be Replaced. 2- If You Had To Install New Battery, All Your Warning Lights Will Come On. After Installing Battery, (Drive Car First For A Few Minutes, Sometimes This Works..) If Not...You Do A "Hard Restart". 3- Proceed With "Hard Restart".  With Push Start Hondas, Press Button Only Once, Wait Until Lights Light Up On Dash Board And Honda Emblem Lights Up. On Hondas With Ignition Regular Key, Turn Key To On Position, Then, Press Radio Power Button And Hold For About 5 Seconds Until You See A Message Asking You To Reboot System.  Click "Yes" Then Release, Lights Should Go Off Then Back On. Try Starting Your Car Again.  If This Does Not Work....4- Open Hood, Disconnect Battery Cables. Begin With The Negative Battery Cable First!!! (The Black Color One, Usually) With The Battery Sensor. Then... Disconnect Positive Battery Cable, (,The Red One) .. Just Make Sure Both Cables Are Away From Battery Terminals. Then,  Allow Both Battery Cables To Touch Each Other For About 10 To 15 Seconds. Remember Keep Both Cables Away From Battery. Then, After 15 Seconds, Release Both Battery Cables. Then, Begin, Connecting Postive Cable First, The Red One To The Postive Side Of Battery Terminal( The Plus Sign) Then, Connect The Negative Battery Cable(The Black One) To The Negative Or Minus Sign Of Battery Terminal. Make Sure Both Cables And Battery Terminals Are Clean And No Corrosion Is Present. Use A 10 Millimeter Wrench Or Socket To Do This And Once You Reconnect Both Cables To Battery Maje Sure They Are Tight. Do Not Over Tighten Cables Or You Will Break Terminals. Warning: Do Not Touch With Your Wrench Any Metal Surface Of Your Car While Doing This Job Or You Will Cause Serious Damage Or Get Hurt.
